title: Choose a palette that fits a brief
claim: With Jev, an agent can recommend one of your described color palettes for a design brief.

example.situation: A creator asks for a calm, readable workspace with one restrained accent.
example.input: The agent supplies three approved palettes with names, hex values and plain-language descriptions.
example.result: Jev returns a palette ID or review. The app renders a preview and checks contrast in code.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Useful when a person already has approved designs and wants a relevant starting point. It does not create a palette or judge an unseen image.

confidence.reason: A builder documents design and palette selection, but no blinded preference comparison is available.

test.dataset: 40 original briefs with three to eight approved palettes, including conflicting preferences and no suitable option.
test.decision: Keep as an optional recommendation only if blind reviewers prefer it to the default without increasing contrast failures.

title: Find the item described by the user
claim: With Jev, an agent can select a supplied item whose description fits a request.

example.situation: A user needs a compact desk lamp with warm light and no subscription-dependent controls.
example.input: The app filters availability and exact constraints, then supplies IDs and descriptions for eligible items.
example.result: Jev chooses an item ID or no match. The agent checks the listed facts before recommending it.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: This selection pattern can serve asset libraries, templates, product catalogs and saved tools. One reusable contract covers several frequent tasks.

confidence.reason: The decision shape appears in demos and official examples. We have no representative item-selection study for the Engine.

test.dataset: 60 authored requests over fixed catalogs, including similar descriptions, missing facts and no-match cases.
test.decision: Require no invented attributes and at least the baseline acceptable-choice rate before making it a default.

title: Give an agent a shorter reading list
claim: With Jev, an agent can rank supplied passages by their relevance to its task.

example.situation: Repository search returns several files for a duplicate-submission bug.
example.input: The agent supplies the bug description and candidate snippets with stable source IDs.
example.result: Jev rates relevance. The agent reads the shortlist first and can retrieve every omitted snippet.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Repeated large tool results can consume a substantial share of a coding conversation. Better ordering could reduce unnecessary reading.

confidence.reason: Two independent studies support testing passage ranking. They do not establish final coding-task quality or cost savings.

test.dataset: 50 debugging or research tasks with labeled relevant passages and counterevidence; keep a fresh evaluation split.
test.decision: Adopt only if final answer quality is no worse within a prespecified tolerance and complete task cost or time improves.

title: Catch a claim the evidence does not support
claim: With Jev, an agent can check a specific claim against a supplied tool result or passage.

example.situation: An agent says a release is live, but the output only confirms a successful build.
example.input: The caller supplies the exact claim and current build and deployment evidence.
example.result: Jev returns separate support and contradiction signals. The agent checks missing evidence before stating success.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: A short check can catch premature completion claims in recurring agent workflows.

confidence.reason: Our small diagnostic and a controlled SRE study support testing the pattern. Both expose errors; neither establishes general reliability.

test.dataset: 60 pre-labeled claims covering stale outputs, partial completion, missing evidence and explicit contradictions.
test.decision: Do not default to automatic acceptance. A useful adviser must reduce false confirmations without hiding uncertain cases.

title: Choose a tool from its description
claim: With Jev, an agent can recommend the next tool from the currently available list.

example.situation: The user says to hide the left panel, but the command is named Toggle sidebar.
example.input: The caller supplies available command IDs, their descriptions and the current interface state.
example.result: Jev selects the command ID. The application checks permissions and asks for any required confirmation.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Useful for natural-language command menus and overlapping tools. It adds little when a rule or explicit user instruction already chooses the tool.

confidence.reason: A small command demo and tool prediction study report useful selections. End-to-end task success is still uncertain.

test.dataset: 50 user phrasings over fixed tool inventories, including unavailable actions, ambiguous requests and no suitable tool.
test.decision: Require at least baseline task completion and a measured reduction in total time or host work.

title: Keep useful parts of a long agent session
claim: With Jev, an agent can propose which old tool records to retain for the next task step.

example.situation: A long debugging session contains repeated file reads alongside one failed attempt that must not be forgotten.
example.input: The caller supplies bounded records and the current goal while preserving the original session.
example.result: Jev recommends keep or review. The agent can recover all records and retains instructions through deterministic rules.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Context pressure is common for frequent coding-agent users. A reliable selector could make long tasks easier to continue.

confidence.reason: Firsthand Reddit enthusiasm and conflicting X previews establish interest, not successful compaction or lower total cost.

test.dataset: 20 consented or purpose-authored long sessions, each with later questions about decisions, constraints and failed attempts.
test.decision: Do not automate destructive history edits. Retain the experiment only if task continuity matches the baseline and total cost or time improves.

title: Choose a useful diagnostic check
claim: With Jev, an agent can rank proposed tests against current failure evidence.

example.situation: A service is unreachable even though its processes look healthy.
example.input: The agent proposes candidate causes and read-only tests, with a current state snapshot.
example.result: Jev recommends a test or review. The agent runs the test, updates its hypothesis and verifies repair invariants.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Repeated incident and debugging work contains many choices about which evidence to collect next.

confidence.reason: The SRE study measured more passing attempts overall, with regressions. Trace attribution also showed low joint diagnosis accuracy.

test.dataset: 30 reproducible local failures with known causes, misleading logs and cases where the correct hypothesis is omitted.
test.decision: Require better task outcomes or fewer diagnostic calls without more incorrect repairs. Report omitted-hypothesis failures separately.

title: Flag records that might describe the same item
claim: With Jev, an agent can compare two descriptions and recommend match, different or review.

example.situation: Two catalogs list the same lamp under different names, but a second pair differs by voltage.
example.input: The caller supplies IDs and relevant attributes for one pair.
example.result: Jev gives a match recommendation. The app checks exact identifiers and preserves conflicting attributes before any merge.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Could reduce manual review when records use inconsistent names. False merges make review important.

confidence.reason: TypeSafe has a worked alignment example. We have not reproduced it or evaluated our generic recipe.

test.dataset: 100 record pairs with human labels, near-duplicate variants and missing identifiers.
test.decision: Require no increase in false merges over the chosen baseline. Keep uncertain pairs separate.

title: Check a draft against named writing rules
claim: With Jev, an agent can flag specific writing issues before revising the text.

example.situation: A product description uses vague claims and never says what the app does.
example.input: The caller supplies the draft and separate rules for clarity, specificity and actionability.
example.result: Jev returns advisory checks. The writing agent revises the draft and a reader reviews the result.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Repeated editorial checks may be useful when a team has explicit rules, including the Unslop rules used in this project.

confidence.reason: Official guidance proposes semantic linting. We have no blinded study of these writing checks.

test.dataset: 40 original paragraphs with blind human labels per rule, including intentional quotations and technical prose.
test.decision: Keep only rules with useful agreement and low false-positive rates. Do not combine them into an unexplained writing score.

title: Choose a category in a large catalog
claim: With Jev, an agent can navigate a described category tree to select a known label.

example.situation: An incident needs one of hundreds of service and issue categories.
example.input: The caller supplies a meaningful hierarchy, a question and the incident description.
example.result: Jev selects a path within a call budget or requests review.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Useful when categories are semantic and the input does not already contain a usable ID.

confidence.reason: The current 320-category experiment is synthetic, and a deterministic parser solved every case.

test.dataset: 60 natural descriptions over a fixed hierarchy, with ambiguous siblings and no category fit.
test.decision: Keep the hierarchy only if it beats the parser or rules on natural descriptions within the same call budget.

title: Prioritize logs for deeper analysis
claim: With Jev, an agent can suggest which supplied log records deserve closer inspection.

example.situation: A diagnostic bundle contains repeated routine events and one unusual warning.
example.input: The caller marks protected records and supplies IDs, severities and bodies.
example.result: The service advises on inspection priority while the caller retains the full archive.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: May help some noisy workloads, but our conservative study added cost and simple severity protection explained an apparent win.

confidence.reason: The available first-party study does not demonstrate net savings.

test.dataset: 50 incident bundles with incident-level labels, repeated records and relevant low-severity clues.
test.decision: Reject any policy that hides a critical clue. Require demonstrated downstream savings before selling it as a cost feature.

title: Choose a recorded response or silence
claim: With Jev, an application can recommend a prerecorded reaction from the currently eligible cues.

example.situation: A player returns to a room after hearing its introduction.
example.input: The game removes completed cues and supplies current facts, timing and remaining recordings.
example.result: Jev recommends a cue or silence. The game rejects stale advice and owns playback.
example.label: Illustrative example, not a recorded result.

value.reason: Could improve the timing and variety of authored reactions without generating new dialogue.

confidence.reason: The optional game integration exists, but no independent playthrough study establishes a better experience.

test.dataset: 20 scripted playthrough paths plus human review, covering return visits, waiting, interruptions and scene changes.
test.decision: Keep narration optional. Require no repeat or stale-playback regression and a clear preference in reviewed playthroughs.
